options: Earth passing between the Sun and the Moon
The Moon passing directly between the Sun and Earth
The Moon's phase changing to New Moon
Earth's shadow reaching the Moon
questions.explanation: A solar eclipse happens when the Moon moves directly between the Sun and Earth, briefly blocking sunlight from part of Earth's surface.
questions.misconception: "Earth's shadow reaching the Moon" describes a lunar eclipse — the two eclipse types are commonly swapped for each other.

questions.prompt: Why don't we get a solar and lunar eclipse every single month, even though the Moon lines up roughly like a New/Full Moon every month?
options: The Moon is usually too far away
The Moon's orbit is tilted about 5.1°, so it usually passes above or below the exact alignment line
The Sun only shines directly at Earth a few times a year
Earth's rotation prevents eclipses most months
questions.explanation: The Moon's orbit is tilted relative to Earth's orbit around the Sun. Most months the Moon crosses the Sun-Earth line a bit above or below it, missing the near-perfect alignment an eclipse needs.
questions.misconception: Distance is a natural first guess, but the Moon's distance barely changes month to month — the tilt of its orbital path is the real reason eclipses are rare.

questions.prompt: What is the difference between a total and a partial eclipse in this model?
options: They are the same thing with different names
A total eclipse only happens for solar eclipses
A closer (smaller) alignment offset produces a stronger, more total eclipse
A partial eclipse is always a lunar eclipse
questions.explanation: The closer the alignment is to perfectly in-line (a small offset), the more completely the shadow lands on its target — a total eclipse. A looser alignment only produces a partial eclipse, or none at all.
questions.misconception: "Total" and "partial" sound like fixed categories tied to eclipse type, but both solar and lunar eclipses can be total or partial — it depends entirely on how precise the alignment is that particular time.

options: The Moon passing between the Sun and Earth
Earth passing directly between the Sun and the Moon, casting its shadow on the Moon
The Moon reaching its New Moon phase
Clouds blocking the Moon from view
questions.explanation: A lunar eclipse happens when Earth moves directly between the Sun and the Moon, so Earth's own shadow falls on the Moon's surface.
questions.misconception: It is easy to swap this with the solar eclipse alignment — the key is which body is in the middle: Moon in the middle means solar, Earth in the middle means lunar.

questions.prompt: Which is safe to look at directly with just your eyes — a lunar eclipse or a solar eclipse?
options: A lunar eclipse — it's just the Moon dimming in Earth's shadow, as safe to view as any normal Moon
A solar eclipse — it's always perfectly safe to stare at the Sun during one
Neither is ever safe to look at
Both need identical eye protection at every moment
questions.explanation: A lunar eclipse is safe to view with the naked eye, exactly like an ordinary Moon. A solar eclipse involves looking toward the Sun and needs certified solar filters at all times except the brief seconds of a total eclipse's totality.
questions.misconception: Because both events are called "eclipses," it's easy to assume the same safety rules apply to both — but only solar eclipses involve looking anywhere near the Sun.
